why: 'neither here nor there' means 'unimportant/irrelevant', not 'not clearly one thing or another'; false synonym for (e)

set.origin: An old idea also found in Latin writers; in English it appears in Chaucer's 'The Knight's Tale': 'To maken vertu of necessitee.'

why: 'first recorded in the Knight's Tale' is not secure: Chaucer also uses it in Troilus and Criseyde (Book IV), which may be earlier, and the idea is older in Latin

set.origin: An ancient Greek saying; best known in English from Longfellow's 1846 translation of Friedrich von Logau: 'Though the mills of God grind slowly, yet they grind exceeding small.'

why: English form existed before Longfellow (George Herbert, 'God's mill grinds slow but sure', 1652); 'known in English from' overstated
